en: Tested those favored by fortune.
Their exceptional and consummate courage
Became known to the sorcerers.
From among the countless multitude, one man—
“This one will do,” they said yesterday—
Was inscribed in the register
Of ill-omened Bilgich.
About a hundred men destined to go
Were entered upon his roll,
And thus the accursed Kite
Was recognized as khan.
They dressed them in the finest coats,
So stout that embers could not burn through them,
And mounted them on fleet horses
That no bird could overtake on a journey.
Whoever offered resistance
They seized and put to rest.
The sorcerers chose one man
And made Chongbilgich khan,
Raising an uproar with their idol,
And in seething Beijing
They made a tumult never to be forgotten.
The treacherous Chinese settled down,
And over the Chinese people of forty khans
The precious Kite became khan.
Both reins and the single bridle
The hero Kite took in hand,
And in Khan Esenkhan’s place
He remained as sovereign.
He gathered an army to take revenge,
And assembled a host of champions.
He draped armor over his back,
And the frenzied wretch
Gave him a hundred sorcerers as companions
And sent Bilgich on his way.
On broad-rumped steeds with spade-like hooves,
Thoroughbreds bred upon the open steppe,
They rode handsome horses,
Knotting their horsehair tails tight,
And making all their gear ready.
Each man strapped on
Six copper cauldrons of provisions.
They circled the black mountains of Kaspang,
Showering hail upon the foothills,
And drawing black mist across the level plain.
From the summits of mountain after mountain
The layered fog broke apart,
So that in especially suspicious places
No person might detect them,
He poured six streams of glacial snow from the sky.
The sorcerous swine’s
Weather-working power was revealed,
Everything shimmered and shook evenly,
And the grasses of the earth parted.
A blinding ground mist
Poured close over the earth,
And from every side, bitterly whistling,
A cold wind broke forth.
Wherever one looked across the hills,
Water surged and flooded,
While all the deserts and plains
Were covered in an impenetrable vapor.
His ferocity became known
When Chongbilgich turned the clouds,
And bewitched the sun and weather.
Every living creature
Whose death was due was overtaken,
While all whose hour had not come
Entered their dens and escaped.
All the jagged mountains
Were caught and wrapped in white snow,
While the grazing wild asses
Fled into the desert and escaped.
His force numbered a hundred men,
And they loaded the warriors’ steeds
With provisions.
They drew arrows loosely from their bows,
And the accursed one whose soul was spent
Took all his sworn companions with him.
Some were skilled at finding the road,
And among the champions he had tested,
Each possessed the strength of a thousand men.
Their courage was mighty and their venom strong;
Such is the nature of a holy war,
And hardship came upon precious lives.
The heroes rode in splendor,
While strings of inverted beads
Glittered upon their heads.
Precious stones hung there,
Revealing their Chinese appearance,
And glass lenses gleamed before their eyes.
Black hair like a resting camel
Shone across their broad shoulders.
Their long trousers and ample breeches
Were fashioned from the hides
Of sixty he-goats,
With the trouser legs plainly visible.
Chasing wild asses and shooting ibex,
The frenzied swine
Plunged deep into their sport.
They watched the approaches and surveyed the land,
Raising a clamor when they climbed a ridge.
They held a rank above ordinary men,
For bloodshed alone
Those ill-omened ones had prepared.
Those who had ridden out from Beijing
Were infidels of uncommon courage,
Each a warrior worth a thousand men.
They raged at the very word “enemy,”
And rejoiced at the mention of death,
Heroes who roamed the world,
Warriors who could find no rest.
Along Kapsang grew black juniper;
They threaded their way beside the black junipers,
And with their dark mass of countless souls
They roamed through the gold mines.
They skirted the mountains of Chai-Algan,
Following the course of Karshan,
Crossing many a humped mountain
And fording many a bare ravine.
They wearied their horses and surveyed the land,
Covering vast distances and raising a clamor,
Chasing wild asses and shooting ibex,
And reveling deeply in many pleasures.
Along the myriad roads from deepest Beijing
They came traveling by night,
From gloomy Beijing
They came traveling by day.
Through gorges trodden only by wild boars
They journeyed without fear,
Across flats where even foxes never roamed
They rode their horses hard and far.
The moon waned and the days passed,
And many days went by.
The horses grew restless and pent up,
While all the heroes found their rhythm.
They never halted by day,
Nor took their daylight rest.
A dark ridge appeared,
A crumbling slope where no goat could pass;
They descended the broken slope,
And along the hills lay At-Oinok.
They crossed At-Oinok and now made camp,
On this side of At-Oinok,
Beyond Echki-Ölbös,
At the projecting nose of the towering mountain,
Upon the spur of the ninth ridge.
When they reached Ak-Urchuk,
A dreadful ordeal unfolded.
Chongbilgich took the lead
And sent roaring fog before them.
His fury seized him fiercely,
And in a raging fit the wretch
Worked his spell upon the sun and weather.
Boz-Talaa, the broad back of the earth,
Lay across the gray plain.
It was a curse upon the open flank,
A road from which none returned,
The vast earth-trap of Kordoi,
Where no human ventured
And not a single four-legged beast
Had ever passed or trodden;
It was called Meenet-Talaa, the Plain of Tribulation.
Every living creature
Said, “If I meet it, I am dead.”
Earth was heaped as high as mountains,
And a man who traveled there by day
Had his fortune cut short that very day.
A horse sank to its knees;
Among all the sons ever born
No one had known such hardship.
Sand was piled as high as mountains,
And a person who traveled there by night
Had his fortune cut short that very night.
It was called Boz-Talaa,
And people who happened upon it
Prepared themselves for death.
There were bull-like beasts and camel-like beasts,
Implacable, unyielding predators,
Wild asses frolicking,
And deadly venomous snakes.
There were creatures called börsö,
Things no ear had heard and no eye had seen,
Every sort of unheard-of creature was there.
There were beasts that devoured rhinoceroses and elephants,
And one called Sword-Tail,
Whose name no living soul knew.
They pressed on through the narrow passage,
Encountering a grievously difficult road,
A devilishly cruel road.
When they beheld this plain,
Chongbilgich saw it from afar,
The nobly born Chongbilgich,
And cast his customary weather spell.
The wide world became constricted,
And over all the level lands
Snow rose to the horses’ flanks.
Six were overtaken by death,
While ninety-four remained alive
And escaped that perilous road.
Watching the stars, they corrected their course,
And their lionheartedness became known.
The jagged Ala-Too loomed before them,
And they reached the Ala-Too.
They traveled along the mountain crest,
Pressing on far without halting.
They set lookouts and surveyed the land,
Searching gorges and choosing passes.
They followed the Ala-Too,
Shoeing their ravine-bred steeds,
Until they reached a place from which to scout.
Let us leave this matter here,
And begin the tidings of brave Seytek,
The panther’s son.
All his ancestors were khans,
And from the beginning Khydyr had blessed his line.
His forefather was a mighty champion,
His first ancestor was a hero.
Against the many enemies who came in hostility,
His courage was manifest to all.
Of the foes who faced him,
Blood poured like water.
Wherever he had spent the night,
A shrine rose with a rumble.
From the beginning, God had upheld him.
When extinguished, his line flared anew;
With every death, it multiplied,
And whenever diminished, it broadened.
He was the descendant of a blessed lion,
The tempered point of keen steel,
A precious lion who never faltered,
A gray-maned hero who knew no grief.
He sliced through valleys and turned them to fat,
And when grievously provoked,
He laid even his own kinsmen low.
The peerless sultan Semetey—
This was Semetey’s descendant,
Who grew to manhood among the Zhediger.
He was nurtured by the land and became mighty;
When his wrath was roused,
Black blood flowed down the slopes.
Of the many enemies who fixed him with hatred,
How many were laid to rest!
Brave Seytek, lion-born,
Prepared himself like a panther.
From the fairies came the heavenly steed,
So that precious Seytek,
When he armed himself, might ride against the foe
And strike them without hindrance.
Kulunsur, who came from the fairies,
Whom no wind could overtake at a gallop
And no livestock could match at a walk,
Was broad-chested and wide-breasted,
With a distinct back and a sharp-ridged spine;
When he entered the fray, he stirred up turmoil.
He would not stand still when tethered,
